segments.description: Please welcome Sam Scowen to our Virtual Grand Sam Coaches Conference. He's an accomplished and multifaceted professional in the world of tennis. Sam was the director of tennis at the Royal Sydney Golf Club, and was entrusted with the crucial responsibility of designing and implementing a strategic plan for tennis, while also engaging key internal and external stakeholders at meetings on the needs of club members. In addition to this pivotal role, Sam serves as the tournament director and referee for all club championship events, ensuring the higher standards of competition and fair playing. Sam's journey to this prominent role has been marked with a wealth of experience and leadership. Previously, Sam held the position of director of education at industry leaders in 2023, illustrating a commitment to the growth and development of the tennis community. From 2019 to 2022, Sam served as the Tennis New South Wales Coach Developer and Tennis World Head Coach, taking a lead on-court role. Prior to that, in 2014 to 2018, Sam worked as the Lawn Tennis Association National Training and Assessor, demonstrating a dedication to nurturing the next generation of tennis talent. Sam's extensive qualifications further underscore this expertise with a Bachelor of Honours in Media Studies, providing a unique perspective on the sport. Holding an international coaching qualification from the LTA and also Tennis Australia, and numerous certifications

in coaching and training, Sam is well prepared to lead and inspire within the world of tennis. Furthermore, being an IT-ECA certified education professional in 2023, signifies a commitment to staying at the forefront of education best practice. Today, he's here to talk us through his thoughts around the benefits of the training needs analysis and how to go about conducting one for your business. Over to you, Sam. Welcome to the presentation by industry leaders. My name is Sam Scowan, and I'm looking to take you through a total of 12 slides, which will take no longer than 13 minutes, but is centred around three key objectives. The main aims and objectives of this presentation are to explore the key processes of a training needs analysis, to discover ways which key stakeholders can be engaged, and to develop change management strategies which will help the organisation implement change in the future. You might be thinking, what is a training needs analysis? A TNA is the process of identifying the gap between existing knowledge and skills and the required knowledge and skills. It is commonly used to identify training opportunities within an organisation. A TNA can also look at the changes within an industry, with new innovations that externally influence the market and therefore the business that's operating within it. Referring to the most recent changes across the Tennis Australia national programs

The TNA focuses on three following stages. One, identifying the organisational needs. Two, conducting the training needs analysis, including the work roles and competencies needed to meet organisational needs, and providing advice to the organisation. A well-defined and conducted TNA can bring several benefits, and by highlighting these you can create a greater level of buying from the organisation at all levels. The benefits of conducting a TNA include identifying the knowledge, skills and resources needed in order to implement change. Head coaches and managers often produce a training plan without first considering how the plan links to business strategy or performance. The process maximises training effectiveness by identifying high-priority areas so resources can be allocated efficiently, which in time maximises the return on investment in the workforce, which is an example of action mapping. Motivating employees and engaging them in their work by demonstrating a commitment to their professional development, which commonly increases employee retention rates by identifying and addressing areas of concern to employees. This template helps navigate key discussion points such as why the organisation wants the analysis, expectations of the outcomes, points of contact for the project and a timeframe and budget. There are also situations where change is forced upon an organisation and its staff. Try to think back to a situation that you have encountered in a club or a coaching programme where you were not consulted before the change was implemented. How did this make you feel? Your role within your current organisation might be to manage or implement changes in tennis programmes, for example court sizes or the delivery of cardio tennis, which may impact staff's feelings of being forced into change, which can in turn affect the outcomes of the delivery of training. For example, in a previous head coach role I had, I was leading a team of eight coaches. Some were young, some were old, and the team had a range of personalities and coaching styles. There was a coach who I knew was going to be a problem with implementing change or the change of direction the company was going to. I made sure as project manager I flagged this individual early, which allowed me to plan a specific strategy to change resistance into positiveness.

Using the template can help gain a 360 degree view across a variety of stakeholders, which helps address any resistant points at all. A common cause behind many issues that impact on objectives relate to communication and communication breakdowns. This can result in staff who are disrespectful, uncooperative, or staff who have a lack of understanding about the organisational objectives. Key stakeholders do include members, coaches, players and parents who should all be engaged and informed from the beginning of a TNA. Communication is important for handling change and you should suggest measures to minimise these risks as part of your analysis by following the communication plan template and provide many opportunities to share information with staff and receive feedback. Ask staff for their input and ideas to encourage the feeling of being part of the solution. Going back to the example I previously used, I planned one-to-one meetings with this person who I flagged as a risk. These one-to-one meetings were planned before the larger team meetings, which gave me an opportunity to relate to them on a deeper level and created more opportunities for them to feel involved in the project, as I really did care about their personal perspective. This, in turn, created a better culture within the larger group and they became less of a risk. When conducting the TNA, you should use reliable, appropriate and efficient methods

Use high levels of interpersonal skills and, at the same time, exert your industry experience through the use of surveys, interviews, working groups and work-rolls analysis. When dealing with sensitive data, you should always follow legal, organisational and ethical requirements to gather information and data to assess the current skills and competencies of staff. Communicate recommendations with stakeholders at a high level first. You should provide a report containing clear advice on the training and assessment needs in the preferred format by your client. Don't expect your recommendations to sell themselves. The representatives have not been on the same journey as you, and what is self-evident to you may be unclear to them. Think about how to best sell your recommendations by referring to the costs, the bigger picture, which is commonly the strategic plan. Provide options and non-training solutions. Make it engaging, using graphs and charts wherever possible.

The TNA might potentially become at the start of a leadership role, a lease agreement or a period of contractual work. You should obtain feedback and comments on the suitability and sufficiency of advice and recommendations. Your presentation of the report may not be the end point. You should encourage feedback about the report to ensure you've provided the best solutions. For example, if any of the recommendations do not align with the strategic and business plan, or do not fall within the proposed training budget, the stakeholders will provide their feedback that may call for changes in your approach. Once these have been agreed and finalized, a final report should be presented to the wider organization in the agreed format, either a PDF or a PowerPoint presentation, for example. Your TNA may uncover the need for change to occur within an organization. The results may bring new perspectives on any cultural issues that may be hindering progress to training. As a leader or project manager, your role is instrumental to change management. Change often causes issues such as conflict, as an organization may move from one cultural way of practice to another. For example, the fear of the unknown, not understanding what is happening, or feeling unsettled because things are no longer done the way they used to be. In summary, implementing change within an organization is not an easy process. Within every leadership role I've had, either as a head coach, tennis manager, or tennis director, the roles have been associated with growing participation or improving member experience through the development of programs, which all involve change and engagement with stakeholders. There have been some key learnings along my career in tennis, however I highly recommend following the key processes discussed in this presentation to give you the best chance in delivering change.
